item.title: Mixed-Acid Bath Analysis and Control Standard
item.description:
Project overview

Item Description
Period Jul 2017–Jun 2018
Scope Mixed-acid anodizing baths for OLED equipment parts
Initial signal Etch-rate, particle, crack, appearance, and Hi-Pot issues returning after about three months
Direct scope Analysis-log/product-defect comparison, sampling revision, repeated component analysis, external-lab correlation, Korea rollout, China revalidation, and training
Completion Redesigned analysis, replenishment, product-sample, and bath-replacement decision criteria

The legacy titration value remained within its control range while product-film performance declined with bath age. The core issue was a single neutralization value converted by the original blend ratio, which did not detect different component-consumption rates and cumulative composition drift.

item.title: 2170 Can Second-Source Qualification
item.description:
Project background and objective

Planned production volume could not remain dependent on one can supplier, so an alternative source had to be qualified. The candidate can differed from the incumbent in alloy ratio, bottom thickness, dimensional tolerance, burrs, and surface condition. Even when component dimensions were within tolerance, those differences could affect beading and crimping geometry, sealing, can-cap laser welding, and vent safety.

As the lead process-validation engineer, I connected drawing and certificate review, incoming-inspection criteria, reset of the existing assembly conditions, sample-cell builds, sectioning and teardown, internal quality and safety tests, and cell-performance evaluation. Purchasing owned supplier, quotation, and order changes; quality owned incoming and outgoing disposition plus the official report; cell engineering owned formation, capacity, and life evaluation; production supported lot-level sample builds.

item.title: New Process Development for Short-Circuit Prevention
item.description:
Project background and problem definition

During early NCM pilot production, ultrasonic pre-welding repeatedly produced positive-electrode uncoated-edge tearing, active-material shedding around the negative heavy edge, and shorts. Reducing the welding condition lowered damage but also weakened the required joint. Manual pre-forming showed a workable direction, but position, pressure, and R geometry changed by operator.

Process decision: I rejected a condition compromise that traded joint strength for lower damage. The selected direction retained the pre-welding requirement, separated the damage mechanism by electrode, and controlled forming position and geometry through a pilot jig.

item.title: 2170 Tabless Cell Development (Pilot Level)
item.description:
Project overview

  • Development task: Build a 2170 A sample using a tabless structure that connects the electrode and collector over a broad area instead of a conventional lead tab
  • Quality process: Company development flow based on IATF 16949: PROTO (A Sample) → PILOT (B and C Samples) → MP (CCB.PO) → SOP (mass production)
  • Completed gate: PROTO A-sample manufacturing and cell evaluation completed
  • Manufacturing constraint: No dedicated tabless equipment or jig; the route had to combine existing 4695 laser equipment with controlled manual work
  • Critical CTQs: Joint condition, internal laser entry and separator damage, insulation and shorts, IR, formation, capacity, and life
  • Direct scope: Early process design, 4M risk analysis, DFMEA, temporary 3D-printed jigs, laser and assembly conditions, sectioning, teardown, and cell evaluation
  • Final result: Compressed and separated failure modes across about 100 trials and confirmed build and functional feasibility through cell evaluation on five functional samples

IATF 16949-based development gates and current position

Quality stage Company sample or approval Technical objective Tabless project status
PROTO A Sample Confirm build feasibility, safety CTQs, and basic cell function for the new structure Completed — cell evaluation on five functional samples
PILOT B and C Samples Verify dedicated jigs/equipment, repeatability, inspection reproducibility, and productivity Transferred as follow-on design items
MP CCB.PO and C Sample Obtain technical production approval for the pilot conditions Follow-on gate
SOP Mass-production start Operate approved conditions in regular production Follow-on gate

The Tabless objective at PROTO was to build the new structure in actual cells and confirm safety and functional feasibility. The results were organized as equipment, jig, process, and inspection requirements for the subsequent PILOT B/C sample stages.

item.title: LFP Power Cell Development
item.description:
Project overview

  • Development task: Develop a 25P LFP power cell on the existing 2170 cylindrical assembly line with changes in electrolyte, clad tabs, turn count, and can geometry
  • Quality process: Company development flow based on IATF 16949: PROTO (A Sample) → PILOT (B and C Samples) → MP (CCB.PO) → SOP (mass production)
  • Customer CTQs: Capacity, IR, and cycle life
  • Direct scope: Change and CTQ definition, 4M risk analysis, Taguchi condition matrices, sample builds, process decisions, trial production, and customer qualification
  • Completed gate: PROTO, PILOT, and MP technical approval completed; SOP remained the subsequent production-start gate
  • Final result: About 20,000-cell trial production, customer qualification and CCB.PO approval, plus completed process, inspection, and production-handoff documents

IATF 16949-based development and production-handoff gates

Quality stage Company sample or approval Technical objective Method Project result
PROTO A Sample Establish build feasibility, CTQs, and measurement criteria for the changed materials and structure DMADV Define and Measure, change analysis Confirmed complete assembly feasibility and basic inspection
PILOT B Sample Screen critical process factors and optimize conditions 4M risk analysis and Taguchi DOE Compressed candidate conditions for impregnation, welding, sealing, and inspection
PILOT C Sample Confirm upstream/downstream linkage and trial producibility of selected conditions Confirmation runs, lot and cell evaluation Established conditions for about 20,000-cell trial production
MP CCB.PO and C Sample Obtain technical approval against customer CTQs and process evidence DMADV Verify and customer qualification Obtained customer qualification and CCB.PO approval
SOP Mass-production start Operate the approved conditions in regular production Work standards, QCP, P-FMEA, and inspection criteria Transferred from MP approval to the production-start gate

The A, B, and C samples were not merely chronological builds. Each stage had a distinct quality decision and entry condition for the next gate. The 25P project completed PROTO and PILOT and reached MP technical approval through CCB.PO.

item.title: Diffuser Scale-Up Production-Introduction Failure
item.description:
Project overview

Item Description
Period Oct 2018–Dec 2019
Type National R&D project for stripping and reuse of an aluminum diffuser
Direct scope Lab and full-part trials, condition-based samples, roughness/microscope/SEM–EDS/particle analysis, and scale-up risk disposition
Goal Shorter process and less high-pressure-water work while retaining surface quality, particles, and reusability
Final decision Scale-up stop, return to the legacy process, and future R&D stop criteria

1. Process-condition transition

Stage Process configuration Work time Quality state
Legacy Bead blast, chemical, high-pressure/manual work, cleaning, and drying About three days Existing reuse criteria
Initial limited trial Existing stripping chemical plus ultrasound About eight hours Removal feasibility
Scale-up Water, ultrasound, high-pressure water, and manual work About one and a half days Erosion, particle, and reuse failure

The scale-up equipment did not include the fume-exhaust infrastructure required for chemical use. Removing chemical action increased dependence on ultrasonic impact, high-pressure water, manual work, and equipment residence time.

item.title: Global Equipment-Maker Technical & Quality Audit Approval
item.description:
Project overview

Item Description
Period Dec 2017–Dec 2018
Parts Susceptor- and diffuser-family components for a global CVD/PECVD equipment company
Process scope Etching→bead blasting→oxalic-acid anodizing→material, Hi-Pot, and particle inspection
Direct scope English specification and CTQ analysis, process-change design, Process Flow/Run Sheet/qualification documents, counterpart samples, measurement, audit response, and retest closure
Completion One audit finding closed, technical qualification approved, and about one year of follow-on supply

1. Legacy-process gaps

Process or control Legacy state Gap against customer requirement
Etching and pretreatment Work sequence and inspection points managed separately Mismatch with English specification and submission items
Bead blasting Common conditions and fragmented evaluation records Weak linkage to surface roughness and particle requirements
Oxalic-acid anodizing Internal film settings Weak linkage to thickness, Hi-Pot, acid, and corrosion CTQs
Material and particle checks Individual test records Incomplete process-flow and sample-history linkage
Hi-Pot Equipment, location, repeat, ramp, and sequence differences Internal/customer disposition mismatch
Change documents Independent revisions by process, inspection, and submission Document–field–sample inconsistency

2. Six Sigma Green Belt-based DMAIC

Phase Core work Decision and output
Define Supplier registration, part qualification, process capability, and CTQs Qualification scope and audit items
Measure Run sheets, equipment capability, samples, and measurement baseline Legacy-to-customer gap list
Analyze Etching, bead blasting, anodizing, and Hi-Pot through 4M Process changes separated from alignment items
Improve Product-family process conditions and inspection specifications Process Flow, Run Sheet, and inspection criteria
Verify Customer location, seven repeated readings, aligned sequence, and three retests One technical-audit finding closed
Control Synchronized process, inspection, sample, and document revisions Technical qualification and follow-on production basis

3. Process-level changes and 4M

Analysis target Suspected cause Finding Action
Etching and pretreatment Man·Method·Measurement — Work sequence, inspection timing, and sample history separated Thickness, roughness, appearance, and downstream comparison Process Flow and Run Sheet sequence realignment
Bead blasting Machine·Method·Measurement — Product-family surface requirements not represented Roughness, appearance, and particle comparison Conditions, evaluation items, and anodizing-entry basis reconfigured
Oxalic-acid anodizing Material·Machine·Method — Internal setting and customer CTQs misaligned Thickness, Hi-Pot, acid, and corrosion checks Product-family film conditions and inspection specification redesigned
Hi-Pot Machine·Method·Measurement — Equipment, location, repeat, ramp, and arc-reading differences Three retests on counterpart samples Customer location, seven readings, ramp, sequence, and arc basis aligned
Acid, corrosion, and particles Method·Measurement — Internal results weakly linked to customer capability Internal, external, and customer-result comparison Test conditions, inspection specification, and external correlation
Change control Man·Method — Process, inspection, and submission revisions misaligned Audit check of document/field consistency Process–inspection–sample–document concurrent revision

4. Hi-Pot measurement correlation

Counterpart samples from the same bath and manufacturing condition
→ customer-designated measurement locations
→ seven repeated readings per sample
→ internal/customer equipment comparison
→ ramp time and test-sequence alignment
→ Arc Counter disposition alignment
→ revised counterpart samples
→ three retests under one decision basis
→ closure of one technical-audit finding

Equipment, location, repeat, and sequence differences were removed before changing the process recipe. The three retests then established correlation between internal inspection and customer disposition.

item.title: Collaborative-Robot Assembly Twin and Edge-Vision PoC
item.description:
The problem

Separate demonstrations of robot motion, vision results, PLC sequences, and MES records do not reconstruct what happened to one product.

This education team PoC used a QR serial as the common key across an Indy7 assembly flow, edge-vision inspection, PLC and SCADA, MySQL/MES, and digital-twin state.

Area Public scope
Project type Education team PoC
My role Robot and Digital Twin
Team implementation QR traceability, robot sequence, vision, PLC/SCADA, and MES
Technologies Indy7, Python, YOLO, Raspberry Pi, Hailo, PLC, and MySQL
Current status Education demo complete; plant pilot and long-running E2E unverified

Team output and my individual role are kept separate. I do not present the full team result as a solo achievement, and the original report containing teammate identities is not published.

item.title: GIGA Press Virtual-Factory Expansion
item.description:
What an interviewer should confirm in 30 seconds

Item Scope
Project form A 10-person training-team PoC, not a live GIGA Press installation
Problem Reduce rework caused by first aligning sequences, interlocks, screen tags, and upper-layer data on physical equipment
What I led Overall planning of the topic, problem, scope, architecture, and integration order; final-report writing
Direct hands-on scope The Digital Twin–AI integration structure, including the AI insertion point and authority boundary
Teammate implementation Detailed PLC Ladder/Factory I/O and SCADA/OPC UA implementation
Verified output An integrated Factory I/O–PLC/Ladder–SCADA/OPC UA–web team demo and final report
Not verified Physical GIGA Press behavior, safety PLC, HIL/FAT, production impact, or DQN closed-loop performance

I was not the project manager or the sole developer. The team lead managed schedule, risk, and the final presentation. I led the overall structure and integration order, wrote the final report, and directly worked on the Digital Twin–AI connection. This distinction shows system-level judgement without attributing teammates’ Ladder and SCADA work to me.

Direct hands-on scope Indy7 control, command/state integration between stations, robot programs, and integrated-flow validation
